slides.text:
A tuple groups a fixed number of values into one. The values can have different types, and the size never changes.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.
slides.code:
tuple = (value, value, value)

read one  -> by its position
unpack    -> one name per value

slides.text: A tuple has no plain print format, so the exercises print it with `{:?}`, the debug format.

exercises.title: Weather report
exercises.guide: Group a city, a temperature and a humidity in one tuple, then read parts of it.

chunks.guide: The type is a tuple of types, one per value, in the same order. Two reports of the same shape.
chunks.text:
let report: (&str, i16, u8) = ("Lima", 21, 80);
    let before: (&str, i16, u8) = ("Lima", 18, 85);

notes.text: One type for each value, in order.

chunks.guide: Print the whole tuples with the debug format.
Read values by position, and compare two of them.
chunks.text:
println!("{} {}", report.0, report.1);
    println!("{}", report.1 - before.1);

exercises.title: Tuple fields
exercises.guide: Read one value of a tuple by its position.

chunks.guide: A tuple with no type written. Rust works it out.
A dot and the position read one value. Positions start at 0.

notes.text: Dot, then the position, counted from 0.
Three values, so the last position is 2.

exercises.title: Change a field
exercises.guide: Assign to one field of a mutable tuple.

chunks.guide: A tuple that changes is declared with `mut`.

notes.text: Without it, no field can be assigned.

chunks.guide: Assign to a field by its position, as to a variable.

notes.text: Only this field changes. The others stay.

chunks.guide: Print it.

exercises.title: Mutated fields
exercises.explanation: `order.0` becomes 15. Then `order.1` becomes 3 + 15 = 18, using the new first field. Positions start at 0, so `.1` is the second value.

exercises.title: Fit the values
exercises.guide: Pick the smallest type that holds each value.

slides.text:
Destructuring unpacks a tuple into separate variables with one `let`. The pattern on the left has the same shape as the tuple on the right.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.
slides.code:
let (name_a, name_b) = a_pair

name_a -> the first value
name_b -> the second value

exercises.title: Unpack a tuple
exercises.guide: Split a tuple into one variable per value.

chunks.guide: A tuple to unpack.
A pattern shaped like the tuple goes on the left. Each name takes the value at its position.

notes.text: Three names for three values, in order.

chunks.guide: The values are now plain variables.
A tuple written in place can be unpacked too. Then use the parts.
chunks.text:
let (city, temp) = ("Lima", 21);
    println!("{} is {}", city, temp);

chunks.guide: The right side can compute its values.
chunks.text:
let (low, high) = (value - 5, value + 5);
    println!("{} to {}", low, high);

exercises.title: Unpack in place
exercises.guide: Destructure a tuple written in place, then use the parts.

chunks.guide: The tuple on the right needs no variable of its own.
The parts are ordinary numbers.
Print the parts and the result.
Unpack halves of both numbers at once.
chunks.text:
let (half_w, half_h) = (width / 2, height / 2);
    println!("{}x{}", half_w, half_h);

exercises.title: Skip values
exercises.guide: Keep some values of a tuple and ignore the rest.

chunks.guide: A tuple of an id, a letter and a flag.
Put `_` where a value is not needed. It takes the place without a name.
chunks.text:
let (id, _, done) = job;
    println!("{} {}", id, done);

notes.text: Matches any value and throws it away.

chunks.guide: `..` skips all the values left, however many. It can sit at either end.

notes.text: Skips every value before the name.

exercises.title: Skip in a pattern
exercises.guide: Skip the values the names leave out, in each pattern.

exercises.title: Swap two values
exercises.guide: Swap two variables with one tuple assignment.

chunks.guide: Both need `mut`, because both change.
chunks.text:
let mut home = 3;
    let mut away = 1;

chunks.guide: The right side is built first, from the old values. Then both names are assigned.

notes.text: Reads both old values before it assigns.

chunks.guide: Print them.

exercises.title: Next step
exercises.explanation: The right side is `(2, 1 + 2)`, built with the old values. Then `prev` becomes 2 and `curr` becomes 3.

slides.text:
Tuples compare from the first field on. They are equal when every field is equal, and the first field that differs decides which one is smaller.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.
A tuple can hold other tuples, and `()` is the empty tuple, the value that means nothing.

exercises.title: Nested tuples
exercises.guide: Put tuples inside a tuple and reach into them.

chunks.guide: Two points, each one a tuple of two values.
Chain the positions: first the point, then the value inside it.

notes.text: The second point, then its first value.

chunks.guide: A pattern nests the same way as the tuple.
chunks.text:
let ((x1, y1), (x2, y2)) = segment;
    println!("{}", (x2 - x1) + (y2 - y1));

notes.text: An inner pattern for each inner tuple.

exercises.title: Name the parts
exercises.guide: Print the width and the height of the segment.

chunks.guide: Two versions as (major, minor), with the same values.
`==` is true when every field is equal.
Two versions that share the major number.
`<` compares field by field from the first. A tie moves on to the next field.

notes.text: The first fields already differ, so the rest is skipped.

exercises.title: Which is smaller?
exercises.explanation: The first fields tie, so the second decide: 1 is less than 2. The last field is never looked at.

exercises.title: Empty and single
exercises.guide: The empty tuple, and the comma of a one-value tuple.

chunks.guide: `()` is the empty tuple, a value that holds nothing.
One value needs a trailing comma. Without it, the parentheses only group.

notes.text: The comma is what makes it a tuple.
Only the number 5, wrapped in parentheses.

chunks.guide: Print the three.

exercises.title: Copy a tuple
exercises.guide: Copy a tuple, change the copy, and keep the original.

chunks.guide: A starting point.
A tuple of numbers is copied on assignment. The copy is a separate value.

notes.text: Copies the values. Both stay usable.

chunks.guide: Change one field of the copy only.
The original did not change.
